items.q: Function-calling schemas serve as
choices: Machine-readable contracts: name, description, typed parameters the model must fill
items.explain: The schema is the contract: it tells the model exactly what it may call and with what typed arguments.

items.q: The ReAct pattern interleaves
choices: Reasoning traces with tool actions and observations
items.explain: ReAct: the model reasons about what to do, acts via a tool, observes the result, and repeats.

items.q: The single biggest operational risk of an autonomous agent loop is
choices: Unbounded loops: repeated failing actions burning cost and time
items.explain: Without step caps, timeouts, and checkpoints, agents retry failing actions indefinitely — cost and side effects compound.

items.q: Summarizing conversation history mid-run primarily addresses
items.explain: History grows every turn; periodic summarization keeps the working context within the window without losing the thread.

items.q: You should reach for a multi-agent design when
choices: Subtasks genuinely benefit from specialization and a single agent cannot hold the whole context
You want a more impressive demo
items.explain: Coordination has real cost; multi-agent earns it only when specialization or context limits demand it.

items.q: Least privilege for agent tools means
choices: Giving the agent admin to avoid errors
Each tool gets only the permissions its task needs; destructive tools need confirmation
items.explain: An agent with a delete tool and no confirmation step is an incident waiting for a misread instruction.

items.q: A good agent eval set measures, beyond final task success,
choices: Tool-call efficiency, failure recovery, and safety-constraint adherence
items.explain: Trajectory quality decides production readiness: count the steps, the wasted calls, and the rules it broke along the way.

items.q: The unit of work a coding agent should produce is best described as
choices: A diff: a bounded, reviewable change to the codebase
items.explain: Diffs are reviewable, revertible, and testable — the shape every code-change workflow already understands.

items.q: The strongest verification that agent-generated code works is
choices: The project's tests pass, including tests the agent did not write
items.explain: Tests you did not author are the oracle; the agent's own claims and green first runs prove little.

items.q: Repo-scale agents handle codebases larger than the context window mainly via
choices: Indexing and retrieval: fetch relevant files, not the whole repo
items.explain: Retrieval narrows the working set to relevant code; dumping the repo into the window is expensive and lossy.

items.q: A review agent's false positives should be handled by
choices: Triage: tune signal, keep a human gate, and measure precision over time
items.explain: Noisy agents get ignored; triage keeps the signal useful and the human gate keeps the bar.

items.q: Wiring an agent into CI/CD safely means
choices: Blast radius sized to trust: read-only first, scoped writes behind approvals
items.explain: Agents in the pipeline get the smallest permissions that work, with approvals before anything destructive.

items.q: The most dangerous property of AI-generated code is that it
choices: Arrives confident and idiomatic even when subtly broken
items.explain: Fluent, plausible code with a hidden bug passes skims — which is why the review bar stays human and high.

items.q: A team policy on AI-generated code should at minimum cover
choices: Review requirements, test coverage expectations, and license/secret hygiene
items.explain: Policy answers the real questions: who reviews it, how it is tested, and how secrets and licensed code stay out of it.

assessments.title: Agentic AI for Data Engineers Diagnostic

items.q: The safest default permission for a data agent is
choices: Read-only: queries can read, writes need explicit approval
items.explain: Read-only by default keeps the blast radius at zero-cost queries; every write path gets a human gate.

items.q: Schema linking in text-to-SQL means
choices: Mapping the question's terms to the right tables and columns before generating SQL
items.explain: Correct SQL starts from the correct tables; schema linking grounds the question in the actual database shape.

items.q: Before executing agent-generated SQL in production you should
choices: Validate syntax, dry-run or EXPLAIN, and check cost guards
items.explain: Validation plus a dry run catches syntax errors, runaway joins, and cost blowups before they bill you.

items.q: A pipeline agent handling schema drift should
choices: Detect the change, alert, and adapt mappings under a test gate
items.explain: Drift is expected; the agent's job is to surface it and adapt safely, with tests confirming the new mapping.

items.q: Contract tests in a data pipeline verify
choices: That upstream data keeps the shape and semantics downstream expects
items.explain: Contracts encode assumptions (columns, types, ranges); breaking them fails fast instead of corrupting silently.

items.q: Agent query audit logs exist primarily to
choices: Answer 'who asked what, when' for debugging, cost attribution, and compliance
items.explain: Every agent query is an action on company data; the log is how you debug it, bill it, and prove it was allowed.

items.q: A text-to-SQL eval set should be built from
choices: Realistic questions over the actual schema, with known-correct answers
items.explain: Eval mirrors production: real questions, real schema, verified answers — anything else measures the wrong skill.

items.q: The first question a PM should ask about any agent feature pitch is
choices: What is the measured success rate on realistic tasks, and what does failure cost
items.explain: Demos hide failure rates; shipping requires the measured number and the cost of being wrong.

items.q: An agent's research output is trustworthy when
choices: Every claim cites a checkable source you verified
items.explain: Citation discipline is the whole game: unverified agent synthesis is a rumor with formatting.

items.q: The right first agent feature to ship is usually
choices: A low-risk, high-frequency workflow where failure is cheap and measurable
items.explain: Low-risk wins build the eval muscle and the trust; autonomy is earned one measured pilot at a time.

items.q: Guardrail metrics for an agent feature should be defined
items.explain: You cannot steer what you did not instrument; guardrails are launch criteria, not postmortems.

items.q: Build-vs-buy for agent tooling hinges on
choices: Differentiation: buy commodity orchestration, build where the agent is the product
items.explain: Commodity agent plumbing is rarely the moat; build where your data, workflow, or evals are the advantage.

items.q: When an agent pilot's numbers miss the target, the PM should
choices: Report honestly, diagnose, and decide: iterate, narrow scope, or stop
items.explain: The pilot's job was to produce evidence; honoring a miss is what keeps the next bet credible.

items.q: When a program agent reports status, accountability for the deadline stays with
choices: The human owner — the agent informs, it does not own
items.explain: Agents synthesize and surface; ownership of outcomes is human and stays human.

items.q: The first governance question before an agent touches team data is
choices: What data classification the agent may access, and what it must log
items.explain: Data classification plus audit logging is the gate; everything else is secondary.

items.q: An incident agent's most important constraint is
choices: The human commander stays in charge; the agent assists, never commands
items.explain: Under incident pressure the chain of command is human; the agent follows runbooks and drafts, it does not decide.

items.q: Measuring 'time saved' by an agent honestly requires
choices: A baseline: the same workflow timed without the agent, then compared
items.explain: No baseline, no claim. Honest measurement compares like-for-like with the old way.

items.q: The expand-or-stop decision after a pilot should rest on
choices: Predefined success metrics plus guardrail compliance
items.explain: Decide the criteria before the pilot; the numbers then make the call, not the mood.

items.q: People-data boundaries for management agents matter because
choices: Team trust depends on knowing how their data is used — surveillance dressed as assistance destroys it
items.explain: Assistance that reads as surveillance costs the trust it was meant to serve; boundaries are the product.

items.q: In an agent system-design interview, the strongest opening move is
choices: Scoping the problem: inputs, outputs, success criteria, and constraints — then designing
items.explain: Scope first: interviewers score whether you clarify before you architect.

items.q: Asked 'fine-tune or RAG?', the decision hinges on
choices: Whether the task needs new behavior/knowledge baked in vs grounding answers in retrievable, changing documents
items.explain: RAG grounds answers in live documents; fine-tuning changes behavior and bakes knowledge — different tools, different costs.

items.q: When your whiteboarded agent design hits a failure mode, you should
choices: Name it, bound it with a guardrail, and move on
items.explain: Naming failure modes with mitigations is seniority signal; hand-waving them is the opposite.

items.q: Debugging a failing agent trajectory starts with
choices: Reading the trace: which step's tool call or reasoning first went wrong
items.explain: Traces are the debugger for agents; find the first wrong step and the cause usually follows.

items.q: A strong behavioral answer about an AI failure includes
choices: What broke, your role, what you changed in process afterward
items.explain: Ownership plus a process change is the signal; AI roles especially reward honest postmortems.

items.q: Your portfolio's best evidence of agent skill is
choices: A working agent with a write-up that names its limits and shows the eval
items.explain: Working code plus honest limits plus measured results beats any credential for agent roles.

items.q: Asked about agent safety in an interview, lead with
choices: Concrete controls: least-privilege tools, step budgets, human gates, evals — tied to the system's risks
items.explain: Concrete controls mapped to real risks show engineering judgment; abstractions do not.

items.q: Low-code agent platforms trade
choices: Speed of building against depth of control — governance still required
items.explain: Low-code ships fast for well-scoped tasks; custom logic, eval rigor, and data governance still need engineering judgment.

items.q: A connector's data-access scope should be
choices: The minimum the agent's task needs — least privilege applies to low-code too
items.explain: Over-scoped connectors turn a helpful agent into a data-exposure incident; scope deliberately.

items.q: Testing a prompt flow means
choices: Running representative inputs, checking outputs, and iterating — like software
items.explain: Flows are software: they need test cases and iteration, not one hopeful run.

items.q: The sign it is time to graduate from low-code to pro-code is
choices: The platform's ceiling blocks a requirement — custom logic, scale, or control you cannot configure
items.explain: Graduate on evidence: a concrete requirement the platform cannot meet, not fashion.

items.q: Monitoring a deployed low-code agent should track
choices: Run success/failure, usage, cost, and user feedback
items.explain: Quiet failures are the low-code killer; monitor runs, spend, and feedback or the agent rots silently.

items.q: Vendor lock-in risk in low-code is managed by
choices: Knowing your exit: what is portable, what is proprietary, and what migration would cost
items.explain: You do not have to avoid platforms; you have to know the price of leaving before you need to.
